w: Built in 1877 for Edward Cargill as an Italianate mansion called The Cliffs, designed by Francis Petre and built in concrete by Harry Lyders for 14,000 pounds. Petre fell for Cargill's daughter Margaret during construction; their courtship ended in an 1881 wedding in the villa's own salon. Fire gutted the house in 1892; it later ran as a 1930s restaurant before crumbling into ruins.
s: The architect fell for the owner's daughter mid-build
_facts: Built 1877 for Edward Cargill, originally called The Cliffs
Designed by Francis Petre, built in concrete by Harry Lyders, cost 14,000 pounds
Petre married Cargill's daughter Margaret in the villa's salon, 1 March 1881
Gutted by fire in 1892; ran as a restaurant/cabaret in the 1930s; now ruins

w: A private museum of bones, bone art, ethnographic artifacts and assorted curios, built inside mural artist and sculptor Bruce Mahalski's own Royal Terrace residence. It opened to the public in March 2018, one artist's personal collection turned into a walk-in cabinet of curiosities.
s: A sculptor's private museum of bones and curios
_facts: Private museum of bones, bone art, ethnographic artifacts and curios
Created by artist Bruce Mahalski inside his own Royal Terrace residence
Opened to the public in March 2018

w: Reputedly the world's southernmost permanent synagogue. The Progressive Jewish congregation's first building was completed in 1863, enlarged at an adjacent site in 1881, then replaced by a more modest suburban structure finished in 1965 -- the one still standing in North Dunedin today.
_facts: Reputedly the world's southernmost permanent synagogue
First synagogue built 1863, enlarged 1881, current building completed 1965
Progressive Jewish congregation based in North Dunedin

w: Māori legend casts Mount Cargill and neighbouring Buttar's Peak as one reclining warrior seen from the city below -- Buttar's the head, Cargill the body. Known in Māori as Kapukataumahaka, it rims the long-extinct Dunedin Volcano, whose crater now cradles Otago Harbour, and its summit carries the city's tallest structure.
s: A reclining warrior in the skyline, per Māori legend
_facts: Māori name Kapukataumahaka
Legend: Cargill and Buttar's Peak together form a reclining warrior's body and head
Part of the rim of the extinct Dunedin Volcano, whose crater forms Otago Harbour
Summit holds the Mount Cargill Transmitting Station, Dunedin's tallest man-made structure

w: New Zealand's first purpose-built Orthodox church, raised in South Dunedin in 1911 for a parish of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch. The exterior keeps a plain Gothic Revival, but the interior switches to Byzantine Revival -- a Category II building serving about 50 families with roots in Russia, Greece and Serbia.
_facts: First purpose-built Orthodox church in New Zealand, built 1911
Gothic Revival exterior, Byzantine Revival interior
Historic Place Category II
About 50 families, many from Russia, Greece and Serbia

w: Dunedin's primary Presbyterian church stands on Moray Place, a hundred metres south of the city centre, and is widely rated the most impressive of New Zealand's nineteenth-century churches. Heritage New Zealand lists it Category I.
_facts: Dunedin's primary Presbyterian church
Located on Moray Place, 100m from the city centre
Widely regarded as the most impressive of New Zealand's 19th-century churches
Heritage New Zealand Category I listing

w: Widely regarded as New Zealand's first skyscraper, built 1908-10 by architects Sidney and Alfred Luttrell in the Warehouse Precinct. Plans for five floors topped by a mansard roof grew to seven storeys mid-construction, and the Romanesque facade brought Chicago-school design into an Edwardian city.
_facts: Widely regarded as New Zealand's first skyscraper
Built 1908-10 by architects Sidney and Alfred Luttrell
Plans grew from five to seven storeys during construction
Romanesque facade blends Chicago-school design with Edwardian-era New Zealand architecture

w: New Zealand's oldest history museum, its brief covering the whole of the old Otago Province -- New Zealand south of the Waitaki River -- though its main focus stays fixed on the city of Dunedin itself. A regional settler-history museum that predates every comparable institution in the country.
_facts: New Zealand's oldest history museum
Covers the old Otago Province, south of the Waitaki River
Main focus is the city of Dunedin

w: One of New Zealand's largest museums, next to the University of Otago campus, with natural science and humanities collections from the Otago region and around the world. Its interactive science centre includes a tropical rainforest butterfly house. Renamed Tūhura -- Māori for 'to discover, explore' -- in 2022.
s: A butterfly house inside one of NZ's largest museums
_facts: One of New Zealand's largest museums
Natural science and humanities collections from the Otago region and worldwide
Interactive science centre with an immersive tropical rainforest butterfly house
Renamed Tūhura Otago Museum in 2022 ('to discover, investigate, and explore')

w: A 393m landform north of Otago Harbour, its secondary summit capped by a 1950s monument to the 1940 New Zealand Centennial -- two bronze figures, 'History' and 'The Thread of Life,' nicknamed 'the buddhas' locally for their seated pose. Wartime shortages delayed the commissioned monument by a decade. A stone from Edinburgh, Dunedin's sister city, is set into it.
s: A WWII-delayed centennial monument nicknamed 'the buddhas'
_facts: 393m hill north of Otago Harbour, Māori name Te Pahuri o te Rangipohika
Secondary summit (329m) topped by a 1950s Centennial monument
Bronze figures 'History' and 'The Thread of Life' by Shurrock and Staub, nicknamed 'the buddhas'
Commissioned for the 1940 centenary but delayed by WWII; includes a stone from sister city Edinburgh

w: The Pineapple Track up this 668m hill got its name in the 1920s, when a local grocer guided walkers to the summit and handed out tins of pineapple as a reward -- the empty cans left along the way became unofficial trail markers. Flagstaff, Māori name Te Whanaupaki, forms part of the rim of the extinct Dunedin Volcano alongside neighbouring Mount Cargill.
s: A 1920s guide's pineapple tins became the trail markers
_facts: 668m hill, Māori name Te Whanaupaki
Part of the rim of the extinct Dunedin Volcano
Pineapple Track named for a 1920s grocer-guide who handed out pineapple tins at the summit
Empty tins left along the track served as informal markers

w: Housed in the heritage-listed 1883 Southern Cross Hotel, built by Italian architect Louis Boldini with Victorian classical interiors. It opened as Dunedin Casino in 1999, had its licence suspended for two days in 2006 after gambling-law breaches, and was renamed Grand Casino Dunedin in 2021 to honour the building rather than the business, later winning a Resene Total Colour Award.
s: A 1999 casino inside an 1883 Victorian hotel
_facts: Housed in the 1883 Southern Cross Hotel, heritage-listed since 1989
Built by Italian architect Louis Boldini
Opened as Dunedin Casino in 1999; licence suspended for 2 days in 2006 for gambling-law breaches
Renamed Grand Casino Dunedin in 2021

w: The Anglican mother church of the Diocese of Dunedin stands in The Octagon, the city's central plaza, right beside the Dunedin Town Hall. Heritage New Zealand listed the cathedral Category I on 11 November 1987, cementing its place among the country's most significant historic church buildings.
s: Anglican seat of Dunedin, right in The Octagon
_facts: Anglican cathedral, seat of the Bishop of Dunedin
Located in The Octagon, next to Dunedin Town Hall
Heritage New Zealand Category I listing, 11 November 1987

w: A research library, historical archive and art gallery of national significance, administered by the University of Otago under the Māori name Uare Taoka o Hākena. Its specialist holdings centre on the history of New Zealand and the Pacific, with particular depth on the Otago and Southland regions -- open to the public as one of the country's most important historical research collections.
s: A nationally significant NZ and Pacific history archive
_facts: Research library, historical archive, and art gallery
Māori name Uare Taoka o Hākena; administered by the University of Otago
Specialist focus on the history of New Zealand and the Pacific, especially Otago/Southland
Open to the public
